Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

[[thm-p-adic-completion-agrees-with-the-fraction-field-of-zp]], the $(p)$-adic
completion $\mathbb Z_p$ of $\mathbb Z$ identifies with

$$\{x \in \mathbb Q_p : |x|_p \le 1\}.$$

$$x = \sum_{n=N}^{\infty} a_n p^n,$$

where $N \in \mathbb Z$, $a_N \ne 0$, and each digit $a_n$ lies in
$\{0,\dots,p-1\}$. The zero element has the all-zero expansion.

Relative to the base vertex $[\mathcal O^2]$, a vertex with normalized elementary divisors $(0,n)$ has a chain of length $n$ through $\mathcal O f_1+\pi^j\mathcal O f_2$. If $n>0$, exactly one of its four neighbors has distance parameter $n-1$: in the basis $f_1,\pi^n f_2$ of its representative, the line spanned by $\pi^n f_2$ has inverse image $\pi\mathcal O f_1+\pi^n\mathcal O f_2$, whose homothety class normalizes to parameter $n-1$. Every other line has inverse image with a primitive vector $f_1+t\pi^n f_2$ and second elementary divisor $n+1$, hence parameter $n+1$. At $n=0$ all neighbors have parameter $1$. Therefore the parameter changes by one at each step, and the displayed chain is a shortest path. A cycle would have a vertex of maximal parameter and two distinct adjacent vertices of parameter one less, contradicting uniqueness of the decreasing neighbor. Thus the graph is connected and has no cycle.

Replacing a lattice basis multiplies its determinant by an $\mathcal O$-unit; homothety adds twice an integer to its determinant valuation. Hence type is well defined, and determinant-one matrices preserve it. For an edge with the endpoint of type $0$ first, choose a basis $f_1,f_2$ of its first lattice with second lattice $\mathcal O f_1+\pi\mathcal O f_2$. Its determinant has even valuation. Rescale both vectors by a power of $\pi$ to make that determinant a unit and then multiply $f_1$ by its inverse; neither operation changes the edge, and the resulting change-of-basis matrix has determinant one. This proves transitivity. A determinant-one matrix fixes $[L_0]$ exactly when it preserves $L_0$ (homothety would change determinant valuation unless its scalar is a unit). Within $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathcal O)$, preservation of $L_1$ is exactly $c\in\pi\mathcal O$, proving the stated stabilizer.

The unique shortest edge gallery from $E$ to any other edge changes endpoint types alternately: changing twice at the same endpoint would shorten it. For a gallery proceeding along $L_0,L_1,\ldots,L_n$, the matrices $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\\pi^n b&1\end{pmatrix}$ for $b\in\mathcal O$ fix every earlier vertex and act transitively on the three possible next edges. In the basis $e_1,\pi^n e_2$, the backward edge corresponds to the line spanned by the second basis vector; the other lines are spanned by $e_1+t\pi^n e_2$ for $t\in\mathbb F_3$, and the displayed matrices send $t$ to $t+b$. For the other initial direction the apartment chain is $L_1,L_0,L_{-1},\ldots,L_{-n}$; use instead $\begin{pmatrix}1&\pi^n b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ at $L_{-n}$, which fixes that earlier chain and is transitive on the three forward lines there. Inductively move each gallery onto the corresponding apartment segment while fixing its earlier segment. Hence $I$ is transitive on the edges with each alternating type word. There are three choices at each extension, so the orbit size is $3^n$. Different words have different type sequences or distances and cannot be in the same orbit. By step 2.2 edges identify with $G/I$, so these orbits are exactly the double cosets.

Define length on $W_{\mathrm e}$ as the number of walls separating $A$ from its translate; on $W_{\mathrm{aff}}$ it is Coxeter length, and its zero set is $\Omega$. Thus no arbitrary nongeometric affine Coxeter extension is silently compared with the lattice below.

Choose a parameter function $q:S_{\mathrm{aff}}\to\mathbb R_{>0}$ invariant under conjugation by $W_{\mathrm e}$. A **root datum** is a quadruple $(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consisting of free $\mathbb Z$-modules $X,X^\vee$ of finite rank in perfect duality $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:X\times X^\vee\to\mathbb Z$, finite subsets $\Phi\subseteq X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subseteq X^\vee$, and a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ from $\Phi$ to $\Phi^\vee$, subject to (rd1) $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$; (rd2) the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$ satisfy $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(\Phi^\vee)\subseteq\Phi^\vee$; (rd3) the group $W(R)$ generated by the $s_\alpha$ acting on $X$ is finite. The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V_{\mathbb R}=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V_{\mathbb R}\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\{x:\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0\}$, and a **base** is a linearly independent subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the rational direct sum $\mathbb Q\alpha\oplus\ker(\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle:X\otimes\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q)$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V_{\mathbb R}$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition. The perfect character–cocharacter pairing for a split torus is supplied by [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]; roots and coroots are additional data, not supplied by that lattice lemma.

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with inner product $B$ ([[def-inner-product-space]]). Equip it with the induced norm $\|x\|_B=\sqrt{B(x,x)}$ ([[def-inner-product-norm]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) and metric $d_B(x,y)=\|x-y\|_B$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]); $\mathrm{Isom}(E)$ below means the isometry group for $d_B$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a supplied reduced crystallographic root system spanning $E$ ([[def-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]). For each $\alpha\in\Phi$, put $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/B(\alpha,\alpha)$ ([[def-coroot-and-dual-root-system]]); write $s_\alpha$ for the orthogonal reflection in the hyperplane $B(x,\alpha)=0$ and $W=W(\Phi)=\langle s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\rangle$ for the Weyl group ([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]]). Write $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$ for the root and coroot lattices ([[def-root-lattice-coroot-lattice-weight-lattice-and-coweight-lattice]]), and fix a positive system with base $\Delta=\{\alpha_s:s\in S\}$ ([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]).

For $\alpha\in\Phi$ and $k\in\mathbb Z$, define
$$H_{\alpha,k}:=\{x\in E:B(x,\alpha)=k\},\qquad r_{\alpha,k}(x):=x-\bigl(B(x,\alpha)-k\bigr)\alpha^\vee.$$
Each $H_{\alpha,k}$ is an affine hyperplane: $B(-,\alpha)$ is a nonzero linear functional, and $k\alpha/B(\alpha,\alpha)$ lies in its level-$k$ set. The sets $H_{\alpha,k}$ are the **affine root hyperplanes** or **walls**, and
$$\mathcal A_\Phi:=\{H_{\alpha,k}:\alpha\in\Phi,\ k\in\mathbb Z\}$$
is their **affine wall arrangement**. An **alcove** is a connected component of $E\setminus\bigcup\mathcal A_\Phi$, with the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]).

The **affine reflection group** $W_a$ is the subgroup of the Euclidean isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}(E)$ generated by the maps $r_{\alpha,k}$ ([[def-generated-subgroup]], [[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). The well-definedness obligation for this subgroup is assigned to `lem-cg-affine-reflection-identities-and-local-finiteness`, which verifies that each generator is an isometry. The **coroot translation group** is the image of the homomorphism $Q^\vee\to\mathrm{Isom}(E)$, $\lambda\mapsto t_\lambda$, where $t_\lambda(x)=x+\lambda$.

The $m$ wall lines through the origin separate that plane into the $2m$ sectors of [F1]. Starting at the beginning of the plus block, the positive product is one alternating word of length $m$ and the negative product is the inverse of the other alternating word. The Hecke braid relation makes their product $1$. Every cyclic rotation also has product $1$, since every factor is invertible. Cutting the cycle into the two gallery arcs of the braid move proves equality of their signed products. This also proves the assertion for a residue translated away from the base alcove.

Put $F=\mathbb Q_3$, $\mathcal O=\mathbb Z_3$, and $\pi=3$. Vertices are homothety classes $[L]$ of rank-two $\mathcal O$-lattices in $F^2$. Join $[L]$ and $[M]$ when representatives satisfy $\pi L\subsetneq M\subsetneq L$. This graph is a tree of degree $4$. The type of $[g\mathcal O^2]$ is $v_3(\det g)\bmod2$; it is well defined. The group $G=\operatorname{SL}_2(F)$ preserves types and is transitive on edges with type-ordered endpoints. Write $L_j=\mathcal O e_1+\pi^j\mathcal O e_2$ and $E=([L_0],[L_1])$. Its stabilizer is
$$I=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathcal O):c\in\pi\mathcal O\right\}.$$
The $I$-orbits on edges are indexed by finite alternating words in $s_0,s_1$ (including the empty word), where $s_1$ changes an edge through its type-$0$ endpoint and $s_0$ through its type-$1$ endpoint. An orbit of word length $n$ has $3^n$ edges. These are precisely the double cosets $IgI/I$.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be a reduced based root datum: $X,Y$ are finite-rank free lattices in perfect integral duality, $\Phi\subset X$ is the finite root set, $\Phi^\vee\subset Y$ its coroot set, $\Delta$ a base, and $W_0$ the finite Weyl group ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Its finite simple-reflection set is $S_0:=\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}\subset W_0$; the simple reflections in a chosen base generate $W_0$ ([[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). Write $Q^\vee=\mathbb Z\Phi^\vee\subseteq Y$ for the coroot lattice.

Put $V=Y\otimes_\mathbb Z\mathbb R$. The **canonical affine walls** are $H_{\alpha,j}=\{v:\langle\alpha,v\rangle=j\}$, with reflection $r_{\alpha,j}(v)=v-(\langle\alpha,v\rangle-j)\alpha^\vee$. The base alcove $A$ is the unique alcove in the positive chamber with $0$ in its closure; equivalently $A$ is defined by $0<\langle\alpha,v\rangle<1$ for every positive root $\alpha$. If there are no roots, put $A=V$. For a nonsemisimple root datum the alcoves include the whole common root kernel as a factor. Define $W_{\mathrm{aff}}=Q^\vee\rtimes W_0$, let $S_{\mathrm{aff}}$ be its reflections in the walls of $A$, put $W_{\mathrm e}=Y\rtimes W_0$, and let $\Omega=\operatorname{Stab}_{W_{\mathrm e}}(A)$. The canonical affine Coxeter system and the decomposition $W_{\mathrm e}=W_{\mathrm{aff}}\rtimes\Omega$, including central lattice directions, are proved in [[lem-hh-root-datum-affine-geometry-and-wall-parameters]]. In particular $S_0\subset S_{\mathrm{aff}}$ with the finite Weyl product orders. Define length on $W_{\mathrm e}$ as the number of walls separating $A$ from its translate; on $W_{\mathrm{aff}}$ it is Coxeter length, and its zero set is $\Omega$. Thus no arbitrary nongeometric affine Coxeter extension is silently compared with the lattice below.

Choose a parameter function $q:S_{\mathrm{aff}}\to\mathbb R_{>0}$ invariant under conjugation by $W_{\mathrm e}$. For $s,t\in S_{\mathrm{aff}}$ with finite Coxeter label $m(s,t)$, impose the alternating braid relation with $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)$ to be the quotient of the free associative $\mathbb C$-algebra on $(T_s)_{s\in S_{\mathrm{aff}}}$ by those braid relations and

$$
(T_s-q_s)(T_s+1)=0\qquad(s\in S_{\mathrm{aff}}).
$$

The extended **Iwahori–Matsumoto affine Hecke algebra** is the crossed product $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q):=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)\rtimes\Omega$. Its underlying vector space is $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)\otimes_\mathbb C\mathbb C[\Omega]$, with multiplication $(hU_\omega)(h'U_\eta)=h\,\omega(h')U_{\omega\eta}$. Thus it adjoins symbols $U_\omega$ with $U_\omega U_\eta=U_{\omega\eta}$ and $U_\omega T_sU_\omega^{-1}=T_{\omega s\omega^{-1}}$. Parameter invariance makes each conjugation an algebra automorphism. If $v_s=\sqrt{q_s}>0$ and $N_s=q_s^{-1/2}T_s$, then $(N_s-v_s)(N_s+v_s^{-1})=0$, the symmetric normalization in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]].

This definition asserts neither an Iwahori–Matsumoto basis nor an equivalence with a Bernstein presentation. It does not identify an arbitrary reductive $p$-adic group's Iwahori-fixed category with modules over this algebra; that requires a separate group-specific equivalence.

Let $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)\rtimes\Omega$ be the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra of [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]]. For $w\in W_{\mathrm{aff}}$, let $T_w$ be the product along a reduced expression, and let $U_\omega$ denote the length-zero symmetry corresponding to $\omega\in\Omega$. Then

$$
\{T_wU_\omega:w\in W_{\mathrm{aff}},\ \omega\in\Omega\}
$$

is a $\mathbb C$-basis of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $q>1$ be a real affine-Hecke parameter, viewed as an element of $\mathbb C^\times$, and let $\xi\ne1$ be a root of unity in $\mathbb C$. With quantum characteristic as in [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], $e(\mathbb C,q)=\infty$ and $e(\mathbb C,\xi)$ is the finite multiplicative order of $\xi$. In particular $q\ne\xi$. The statement compares scalar parameter regimes; it asserts no isomorphism, Morita equivalence, or classification relation between the corresponding algebras.

A **root datum** is a quadruple $(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consisting of free $\mathbb Z$-modules $X,X^\vee$ of finite rank in perfect duality $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:X\times X^\vee\to\mathbb Z$, finite subsets $\Phi\subseteq X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subseteq X^\vee$, and a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ from $\Phi$ to $\Phi^\vee$, subject to (rd1) $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$; (rd2) the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$ satisfy $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(\Phi^\vee)\subseteq\Phi^\vee$; (rd3) the group $W(R)$ generated by the $s_\alpha$ acting on $X$ is finite. The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V_{\mathbb R}=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V_{\mathbb R}\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\{x:\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0\}$, and a **base** is a linearly independent subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the rational direct sum $\mathbb Q\alpha\oplus\ker(\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle:X\otimes\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q)$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V_{\mathbb R}$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition. The perfect character–cocharacter pairing for a split torus is supplied by [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]; roots and coroots are additional data, not supplied by that lattice lemma.

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be as in [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]], with finite Weyl group $W_0$. Use the finite simple-reflection set $S_0=\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}$ specified in [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]], where $S_0$ generates $W_0$ and is contained in $S_{\mathrm{aff}}$. For $s,t\in S_0$, let $m(s,t)$ be the order of $st$ in $W_0$, which is finite because $W_0$ is finite. The group algebra $\mathbb C[Y]$ is the complex vector space with basis $\{\theta_y:y\in Y\}$ and multiplication $\theta_y\theta_z=\theta_{y+z}$; its identity is $\theta_0$. The simple reflection corresponding to $\alpha\in\Delta$ acts on $Y$ by $s_\alpha(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$.

Write $2X=\{2x:x\in X\}$. For each simple root $\alpha\in\Delta\cap2X$, also supply a positive scalar $v'_\alpha$; it is the second parameter in the doubled-root rank-one Bernstein relation. This additional scalar is formal input to the presentation. To compare this presentation with a specified $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q)$, its parameters must be **attached**: require $v'_\alpha=v(H_{\alpha,1})$, where $v(H)$ is the positive square root of the parameter of its wall reflection, well defined by [[lem-hh-root-datum-affine-geometry-and-wall-parameters]]. The finite parameter is already $v_\alpha=v(H_{\alpha,0})$. Without this tie one is defining a formal Bernstein algebra, not asserting comparison with the fixed $q$. When $\alpha\notin2X$, no second parameter is used; the wall-parameter lemma proves the two wall classes have equal parameters.

Define the **formal Bernstein algebra** $\mathcal B(R,v,v')$ as the quotient of the free associative $\mathbb C$-algebra on $\{\theta_y:y\in Y\}$ and $\{N_s:s\in S_0\}$ by $\theta_0=1$, $\theta_y\theta_z=\theta_{y+z}$ for $y,z\in Y$, the finite Hecke relations, and the following cross-relation for each $\alpha\in\Delta$ and $y\in Y$. Here $v_\alpha:=v_{s_\alpha}=\sqrt{q_{s_\alpha}}>0$ from [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]], and the finite Hecke relations are $(N_s-v_s)(N_s+v_s^{-1})=0$ for $s\in S_0$ and equality of the alternating products of $N_s,N_t$ of length $m(s,t)$ for distinct $s,t\in S_0$ ([[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]):

$$
\theta_yN_{s_\alpha}-N_{s_\alpha}\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}=\begin{cases}(v_\alpha-v_\alpha^{-1})\dfrac{\theta_y-\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}}{1-\theta_{-\alpha^\vee}},&\alpha\notin2X,\\[1ex]\bigl((v_\alpha-v_\alpha^{-1})+\theta_{-\alpha^\vee}(v'_\alpha-(v'_\alpha)^{-1})\bigr)\dfrac{\theta_y-\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}}{1-\theta_{-2\alpha^\vee}},&\alpha\in2X.\end{cases}
$$

The quotients are interpreted in $\mathbb C[Y]$; their well-definedness is proved in [[lem-hh-affine-hecke-bernstein-quotients-are-well-defined]]. The quotient construction defines an associative algebra. It does **not** assert that $\mathcal B(R,v,v')$ is nonzero, has a PBW basis, or is isomorphic to the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra of [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]].

derivations.claim: By [F1], $s_\alpha(y)=y-n\alpha^\vee$, so by [F2] the numerator is $\theta_y(1-u^n)$. If $n>0$, then $(1-u^n)/(1-u)=1+u+\cdots+u^{n-1}$; if $n=0$, the quotient is zero; and if $n=-k<0$, then $(1-u^n)/(1-u)=-u^{-k}(1+u+\cdots+u^{k-1})$. Each expression is a finite Laurent polynomial, proving the first assertion.

If $\alpha\in2X$, write $\alpha=2\beta$ with $\beta\in X$. Then $n=\langle2\beta,y\rangle=2\langle\beta,y\rangle=2m$ for an integer $m$. With $u=\theta_{-\alpha^\vee}$, the numerator is $\theta_y(1-u^{2m})$. For $m>0$, $(1-u^{2m})/(1-u^2)=1+u^2+\cdots+u^{2m-2}$; for $m=0$ it is zero; and for $m<0$ the same finite negative-power identity from step 1.1, applied to $u^2$, is a Laurent polynomial. Since $1-u^2=1-\theta_{-2\alpha^\vee}$, the second assertion follows.

The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V_{\mathbb R}=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V_{\mathbb R}\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\{x:\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0\}$, and a **base** is a linearly independent subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the rational direct sum $\mathbb Q\alpha\oplus\ker(\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle:X\otimes\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q)$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V_{\mathbb R}$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition. The perfect character–cocharacter pairing for a split torus is supplied by [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]; roots and coroots are additional data, not supplied by that lattice lemma.

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be as in [[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]], with finite Weyl group $W_0$. Use the finite simple-reflection set $S_0=\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}$ specified in [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]], where $S_0$ generates $W_0$ and is contained in $S_{\mathrm{aff}}$. For $s,t\in S_0$, let $m(s,t)$ be the order of $st$ in $W_0$, which is finite because $W_0$ is finite. The group algebra $\mathbb C[Y]$ is the complex vector space with basis $\{\theta_y:y\in Y\}$ and multiplication $\theta_y\theta_z=\theta_{y+z}$; its identity is $\theta_0$. The simple reflection corresponding to $\alpha\in\Delta$ acts on $Y$ by $s_\alpha(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$.

Write $2X=\{2x:x\in X\}$. For each simple root $\alpha\in\Delta\cap2X$, also supply a positive scalar $v'_\alpha$; it is the second parameter in the doubled-root rank-one Bernstein relation. This additional scalar is formal input to the presentation. To compare this presentation with a specified $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q)$, its parameters must be **attached**: require $v'_\alpha=v(H_{\alpha,1})$, where $v(H)$ is the positive square root of the parameter of its wall reflection, well defined by [[lem-hh-root-datum-affine-geometry-and-wall-parameters]]. The finite parameter is already $v_\alpha=v(H_{\alpha,0})$. Without this tie one is defining a formal Bernstein algebra, not asserting comparison with the fixed $q$. When $\alpha\notin2X$, no second parameter is used; the wall-parameter lemma proves the two wall classes have equal parameters.

Define the **formal Bernstein algebra** $\mathcal B(R,v,v')$ as the quotient of the free associative $\mathbb C$-algebra on $\{\theta_y:y\in Y\}$ and $\{N_s:s\in S_0\}$ by $\theta_0=1$, $\theta_y\theta_z=\theta_{y+z}$ for $y,z\in Y$, the finite Hecke relations, and the following cross-relation for each $\alpha\in\Delta$ and $y\in Y$. Here $v_\alpha:=v_{s_\alpha}=\sqrt{q_{s_\alpha}}>0$ from [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]], and the finite Hecke relations are $(N_s-v_s)(N_s+v_s^{-1})=0$ for $s\in S_0$ and equality of the alternating products of $N_s,N_t$ of length $m(s,t)$ for distinct $s,t\in S_0$ ([[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]):

$$
\theta_yN_{s_\alpha}-N_{s_\alpha}\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}=\begin{cases}(v_\alpha-v_\alpha^{-1})\dfrac{\theta_y-\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}}{1-\theta_{-\alpha^\vee}},&\alpha\notin2X,\\[1ex]\bigl((v_\alpha-v_\alpha^{-1})+\theta_{-\alpha^\vee}(v'_\alpha-(v'_\alpha)^{-1})\bigr)\dfrac{\theta_y-\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}}{1-\theta_{-2\alpha^\vee}},&\alpha\in2X.\end{cases}
$$

The quotients are interpreted in $\mathbb C[Y]$; their well-definedness is proved in [[lem-hh-affine-hecke-bernstein-quotients-are-well-defined]]. The quotient construction defines an associative algebra. It does **not** assert that $\mathcal B(R,v,v')$ is nonzero, has a PBW basis, or is isomorphic to the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra of [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]].

Let $R=(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be the reduced based root datum and let $\mathbb C[Y]$ and the reflection action be as in [[def-hh-affine-hecke-bernstein-presentation]]. For every $\alpha\in\Delta$ and $y\in Y$,

$$
\frac{\theta_y-\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}}{1-\theta_{-\alpha^\vee}}\in\mathbb C[Y]\quad\text{if }\alpha\notin2X,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\theta_y-\theta_{s_\alpha(y)}}{1-\theta_{-2\alpha^\vee}}\in\mathbb C[Y]\quad\text{if }\alpha\in2X.
$$

derivations.claim: Translation by $y\in Y$ preserves crossing directions, while its possible permutation of facet types is accounted for by the crossed product. Explicitly write $t_y=w_y\omega_y$ with $w_y\in W_{\mathrm{aff}}$, $\omega_y\in\Omega$. If a gallery for $t_z$ has affine types $s_1,\ldots,s_r$ and terminal frame $\omega_z$, then after translation and removal of the initial affine transport $w_y$ its types are $\omega_y s_i\omega_y^{-1}$, with the same signs. The relation $U_{\omega_y}N_s^{\pm1}U_{\omega_y}^{-1}=N_{\omega_y s\omega_y^{-1}}^{\pm1}$ shows that multiplying its signed product after the product for $t_y$ gives exactly this translated gallery, with terminal frame $\omega_y\omega_z$. Concatenation and [F2] therefore give $\Theta_y\Theta_z=\Theta_{y+z}$. The empty gallery gives $\Theta_0=1$, so $\Theta_y^{-1}=\Theta_{-y}$. If $y$ is dominant, each separating wall is crossed toward $D$ on a minimal gallery to $t_yA$: for every positive root $\beta$, its coordinate changes from $\langle\beta,A\rangle\subset(0,1)$ to that interval translated by the nonnegative integer $\langle\beta,y\rangle$. Thus all signs are positive and $\Theta_y=N_{t_y}$.

Let $h$ be the sum of the positive coroots. A simple reflection permutes all positive coroots except its own, which it negates: in simple-coroot coordinates, reflection in a simple root changes only the coefficient of that simple coroot, so any other positive coroot retains a positive coefficient elsewhere and hence cannot become negative by [F3]. Therefore $s_\alpha(h)=h-2\alpha^\vee$; comparing with the reflection formula gives $\langle\alpha,h\rangle=2$ for each simple $\alpha$. For any $y$, sufficiently large integer $M\ge0$ makes $\mu=Mh$ and $\lambda=y+Mh$ dominant. If there are no roots use $\mu=0$, $\lambda=y$. Step 1.1 now yields $\Theta_y=\Theta_\lambda\Theta_\mu^{-1}=N_{t_\lambda}N_{t_\mu}^{-1}$, proving the asserted formula and its independence of the dominant decomposition. Central lattice directions cause no difficulty because no root inequality involves them.

For $w\in W_0$, a reduced finite gallery from $A$ to $wA$ crosses each of its separating root hyperplanes from its positive side to its negative side. Hence $E_D(w)=N_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$. Translate this gallery by $y$ and concatenate it after a gallery for $t_y$, transporting its types through $\omega_y$ by the crossed-product identity proved in step 1.1. By [F2], $E_D(t_yw)=\Theta_yN_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$. The elements $N_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$ form a basis of the finite Hecke algebra: expansion of each inverse $N_s^{-1}=N_s-c_s$ gives $N_w$ plus strictly shorter terms, and induction on finite Weyl length proves both spanning and independence. Every element of $Y\rtimes W_0$ has a unique expression $t_yw$, so the oriented basis [F2], followed by this finite change of basis separately for each $y$, proves that $\{\Theta_yN_w\}$ is a basis of the full algebra. In particular $y\mapsto\Theta_y$ embeds $\mathbb C[Y]$.

Fix $\alpha\in\Delta$, put $s=s_\alpha$, $a=\alpha^\vee$, $n=\langle\alpha,y\rangle$, and let $D'=sD$. The orientations toward $D$ and $D'$ differ only on the walls parallel to $\alpha$, since a simple reflection permutes the other positive roots by the simple-coordinate argument in step 2.1. Suppose $n\ge0$ and choose a minimal gallery from $A$ to $t_yA$. Its relevant walls are exactly $H_{\alpha,k}$ for $1\le k\le n$, each crossed once toward $D$ and in increasing order of $k$. On these crossings the signed factors for $D,D'$ are respectively $N_i,N_i^{-1}$, whose difference is $c(\alpha,k)$; on the other crossings the factors agree.

Expand $E_D(t_y)-E_{D'}(t_y)$ by telescoping over its relevant crossings, using the $D$ factors before a deleted factor and the $D'$ factors after it. In the term belonging to $H_{\alpha,k}$ replace $N_i-N_i^{-1}$ by $c(\alpha,k)$ and multiply on the right by $N_s$. The remaining signed word represents a gallery obtained by deleting that crossing and reflecting the whole subsequent tail across $H_{\alpha,k}$. Its signs are exactly the $D$ signs: the prefix already has them, while the reflection has linear part $s$ and therefore takes the $D'$ orientation of the suffix to $D$. Before reflecting, the added final crossing from $t_yA$ to $t_ysA$ moves toward $D'$, so its factor is indeed $N_s$. Deleting the crossing keeps the prefix unchanged and reflects the suffix's initial alcove back to that prefix's endpoint; hence this is a genuine gallery, even if it is not minimal. Its framed endpoint is $r_{\alpha,k}t_ys=t_{ka}st_ys=t_{sy+ka}=t_{y-(n-k)a}$. Thus [F2] identifies this term with $c(\alpha,k)\Theta_{y-(n-k)a}$. This explicitly accounts for every other wall crossing carried along in the tail.

Starting with the positive $D'$ crossing from $A$ to $sA$, then reflecting a $D$ gallery for $t_{sy}$, and finishing with the negative $D'$ crossing from $t_ysA$ to $t_yA$, proves $E_{D'}(t_y)=N_s\Theta_{sy}N_s^{-1}$ by [F2]. Therefore steps 4.1–5.1 give $\Theta_yN_s-N_s\Theta_{sy}=\sum_{k=1}^n c(\alpha,k)\Theta_{y-(n-k)a}.$ For $n=0$ the products have identical signs, and the same conclusion holds with an empty sum. This derivation uses only the parameter of the deleted wall, so applies to arbitrary positive affine parameter values.

If $\alpha\notin2X$, [F1] makes all coefficients in step 6.1 equal to $c_\alpha$. Setting $j=n-k$ and summing the geometric progression gives $\Theta_yN_s-N_s\Theta_{sy}=c_\alpha\frac{\Theta_y-\Theta_{sy}}{1-\Theta_{-a}}.$ If $\alpha\in2X$, perfect integral duality gives $n=2m$ for an integer $m\ge0$. Then $j=n-k$ has the same parity as $k$. The coefficients for even $j$ are $c_\alpha$ and those for odd $j$ are $c'_\alpha$. Pairing consecutive terms gives $\Theta_yN_s-N_s\Theta_{sy}=(c_\alpha+\Theta_{-a}c'_\alpha)\frac{\Theta_y-\Theta_{sy}}{1-\Theta_{-2a}}.$ Both expressions mean the finite Laurent polynomials of [F4], with value zero when $n=0$.

For all $y,z$ the expression $D(y)=\Theta_yN_s-N_s\Theta_{sy}$ satisfies $D(y+z)=\Theta_yD(z)+D(y)\Theta_{sz}$ by direct multiplication and step 1.1. Since $D(0)=0$, substituting $z=-y$ yields $D(y)=-\Theta_yD(-y)\Theta_{sy}$. If $n<0$, apply the proved nonnegative-pairing relation to $-y$. In either root case write its common rational coefficient as $C$, namely $c_\alpha/(1-\Theta_{-a})$ or $(c_\alpha+\Theta_{-a}c'_\alpha)/(1-\Theta_{-2a})$. Then $-\Theta_yC(\Theta_{-y}-\Theta_{-sy})\Theta_{sy}=C(\Theta_y-\Theta_{sy}).$ This calculation is valid in the fraction field of the embedded Laurent algebra from step 3.1; both final sides are the finite Laurent polynomials of [F4]. Thus the two Bernstein cross-relations hold for negative $n$ as well.

By steps 1.1 and 7.1–8.1, the elements $\Theta_y,N_s$ satisfy all defining relations of the attached formal Bernstein quotient $\mathcal B$. The finite Hecke relations already hold in the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra. The universal property of the quotient therefore gives a homomorphism $F:\mathcal B\to\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}$ sending its stated generators to those elements.

In $\mathcal B$, every word lies in the span of $\theta_yN_w$. Indeed move lattice factors to the left through finite generators, using the rearranged Bernstein relation $N_s\theta_y=\theta_{sy}N_s+R_y$, where $R_y$ is its Laurent-polynomial error term; this is the defining relation applied to $sy$ with its sign reversed. Induct lexicographically on the number of finite generators and the number of finite-generator/lattice-factor inversions. The leading reordered term reduces the inversion number, and each error term loses one finite generator. Combine adjacent lattice factors and reduce the remaining finite Hecke word by its quadratic and braid relations. These reductions give finite sums, so the induction terminates. Under $F$ the resulting spanning family maps to the basis in step 3.1. A finite kernel relation would therefore have zero coefficients in that basis; and every element of the target has a preimage by that basis. Thus $F$ is an isomorphism and $\{\theta_yN_w\}$ is a basis of $\mathcal B$.

Reversal of words fixing every $\theta_y$ and every finite $N_s$ induces an involutive antiautomorphism of $\mathcal B$. The lattice relations are stable under reversal, as are the quadratic relations and the alternating braid relations. For the cross-relation, its right side has the form $R_y=C(\theta)(\theta_y-\theta_{sy})$ and satisfies $R_{sy}=-R_y$. The defining relation at $sy$, multiplied by $-1$, is $N_s\theta_y-\theta_{sy}N_s=R_y$, precisely the reversed defining relation at $y$; Laurent factors commute on the right side. Hence every defining relation is preserved. This involution sends the basis $\theta_yN_w$ to $N_{w^{-1}}\theta_y$. Inversion permutes $W_0$, so $\{N_w\theta_y\}$ is a second basis. Transporting it by $F$ proves the second ordered basis in $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}$. Every selection, expansion and induction used in the proof is finite; no choice principle is needed.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be any reduced based root datum, and give its canonical extended affine Weyl group arbitrary positive affine Hecke parameters invariant under extended conjugation ([[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]]). Write $v_\alpha$ for the parameter of the finite simple reflection $s_\alpha$. In the formal Bernstein algebra of [[def-hh-affine-hecke-bernstein-presentation]], attach its exceptional parameters to this affine system by requiring $v'_\alpha=v(H_{\alpha,1})$ for $\alpha\in\Delta\cap2X$, where $v(H)$ is the parameter of reflection in the wall $H$.

For $y\in Y$, write $y=\lambda-\mu$ with $\lambda,\mu$ dominant lattice elements. The element
$$\Theta_y:=N_{t_\lambda}N_{t_\mu}^{-1}$$
is independent of these choices and satisfies $\Theta_y\Theta_z=\Theta_{y+z}$. Its values are linearly independent, and both
$$\{\Theta_yN_w:y\in Y,\ w\in W_0\},\qquad\{N_w\Theta_y:y\in Y,\ w\in W_0\}$$
are complex vector-space bases of the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra. The assignment $\theta_y\mapsto\Theta_y$, $N_s\mapsto N_s$ gives an isomorphism from the attached formal Bernstein algebra to the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra. In particular both ordered families $\theta_yN_w$ and $N_w\theta_y$ are bases of the former. No restriction to an irreducible or semisimple datum, to equal parameters, or to parameters greater than one is imposed.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ be a reduced root datum ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Then: (a) $W(R)$ is finite and generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Phi$; for a base $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ it is generated by the simple reflections $s_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$; (b) the correspondences between bases, positive systems and Weyl chambers are bijective, and $W(R)$ acts simply transitively on the set of Weyl chambers, equivalently on the set of bases; (c) for a chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ there is a unique longest element $w_0\in W(R)$ with $w_0(\Phi^+)=-\Phi^+$, and for every $w\in W(R)$ the integer $n(w)=|\Phi^+\cap w(\Phi^-)|$ equals the length of $w$ with respect to the simple reflections, with $n(w^{-1})=n(w)$ and $n(w_0w)=|\Phi^+|-n(w)$; (d) $\Phi$ spans $V=X\otimes\mathbb Q$ iff the root datum is semisimple, and then $\Phi$ is a reduced root system in $V$ in the Euclidean sense.

Let $H$ be the complex affine Hecke algebra of a reduced based root datum with positive real parameters and Bernstein PBW as in [[thm-hh-affine-hecke-general-root-data-bernstein-pbw]]. To keep the page's dual convention explicit, put $L=Y$, $B=\Delta^\vee\subset L$, and write $\beta^\vee=\alpha\in X$ when $\beta=\alpha^\vee\in B$. Thus $A=\mathbb C[L]$ is the Bernstein subalgebra, $T=\operatorname{Hom}(L,\mathbb C^\times)$, and $E=\operatorname{Hom}(L,\mathbb R)=X\otimes\mathbb R$. The Weyl group $W=W_0$ acts on all these objects. Index parabolic subsets by $P\subseteq B$; they correspond bijectively to subsets of $\Delta$ by $\alpha\leftrightarrow\alpha^\vee$.

Write $W_P=\langle s_\beta:\beta\in P\rangle$, and let $H_P$ denote the subalgebra of $H$ generated by $A$ and $N_{s_\beta}$ for $\beta\in P$. In particular $H_\varnothing=A$ and $H_B=H$. The notation $H_P$ here always retains the full lattice $L$. For an $H_P$-module $V$, its **parabolic induction** is $I_P(V)=H\otimes_{H_P}V$ with $H$ acting on the first factor.

All modules in the classification below are nonzero, unital, complex and finite dimensional. For an $A$-module $V$ and $t\in T$, the **generalized weight space** is
$$
V_t=\{v\in V:(\theta_\ell-t(\ell))^{\dim V}v=0\text{ for every }\ell\in L\}.
$$
The **weight set** is $\operatorname{Wt}(V)=\{t:V_t\ne0\}$. The logarithmic absolute value $\lambda(t)\in E$ is $\lambda(t)(\ell)=\log|t(\ell)|$. For an irreducible $H_P$-module, the **central weight character** $\operatorname{cc}_P(V)$ is its $W_P$-orbit of $A$-weights; the fact that there is exactly one such orbit is proved in [[lem-hh-affine-hecke-parabolic-weight-filtration]]. This terminology specifies the character of $A^{W_P}$; no equality with a larger center is needed.

Use $L,B,E,W,H_P,T$ from [[def-hh-affine-hecke-parabolic-subalgebras-and-central-characters]]. Fix a positive definite $W$-invariant inner product on $E$, obtained by averaging any positive definite form over the finite group $W$ ([[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). For $P\subseteq B$ put
$$
E_P=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\beta^\vee:\beta\in P\},\qquad E^P=E_P^\perp=\{\nu:\beta(\nu)=0\text{ for every }\beta\in P\},\qquad K_P=-\sum_{\beta\in P}\mathbb R_{\ge0}\beta^\vee.
$$
In particular $K_\varnothing=\{0\}$. Set
$$
C=\{\nu\in E:\beta(\nu)\ge0\text{ for all }\beta\in B\},\qquad C_P^{++}=\{\nu\in E^P:\beta(\nu)>0\text{ for all }\beta\in B\setminus P\}.
$$
A finite dimensional $H_P$-module is **tempered** if all its logarithmic weights belong to $K_P$. It is **essentially tempered with real exponent $\nu$** if $\nu\in E^P$ and every logarithmic weight belongs to $\nu+K_P$. For a nonzero module this exponent is unique because $E^P\cap E_P=0$. An irreducible essentially tempered module is in **strictly positive position** if $\nu\in C_P^{++}$. A **Langlands datum** is a pair $(P,\sigma)$ with $\sigma$ such a module. Its **standard module** is $I_P(\sigma)$.

These are the weight definitions of temperedness and essential temperedness; no analytic characterization is presumed. For the full algebra the tempered condition is equivalently $|t(\ell)|\le1$ for every weight $t$ and every $\ell\in L^+=\{\ell:\langle\ell,\beta^\vee\rangle\ge0\ (\beta\in B)\}$. The equivalence follows because this rational polyhedral cone is generated as a real cone by its lattice points, and its polar cone is $K_B$. For $H_P$ use $P$ in place of $B$. The lattice-point assertion follows by expressing the cone as its central linear space plus nonnegative rational fundamental-weight rays and clearing denominators. The polar assertion also follows directly by expanding in the basis of simple coroots and testing the dual fundamental weights and both signs of every central vector.

The definition includes the whole central real exponent: when $P=B$, strict positivity imposes no additional inequality and $C_B^{++}=E^B$. Unitary central characters remain part of $\sigma$. Thus no uniqueness of a choice of unitary twist or of a semisimple-parabolic torus factorization is asserted.

derivations.claim: Every right coset of $W_P$ has a minimal-length representative $w$; minimality gives $w(P)\subset R_L^+$, since otherwise right multiplication by a corresponding simple reflection decreases its inversion number. Such a $w$ sends all positive subsystem roots to positive roots. Along a reduced word for $v\in W_P$, inversion numbers therefore increase at each step of $wv$, giving $\ell(wv)=\ell(w)+\ell(v)$. Conversely this equality shows $w$ is the unique minimum in its coset: if $u=wv$ were another minimum its length would be $\ell(w)+\ell(v)$, forcing $v=1$. Thus $W^P$ is exactly this set of representatives. Applying [F1] to finite products and the cross-relations shows $H_P$ has basis $N_v\theta_\ell$ for $v\in W_P$, $\ell\in L$: these elements span the subalgebra because cross-relations and finite Hecke multiplication keep all finite Weyl indices in $W_P$, and are independent as a subset of the PBW basis of $H$. The length-additive factorization $N_{wv}=N_wN_v$ now proves $H=\bigoplus_{w\in W^P}N_wH_P$. Tensoring gives $I_P(V)=\bigoplus_{w\in W^P}N_w\otimes V$, including the injected identity summand, which is $H_P$-stable.

citations.quote: Let $q>1$ be a real affine-Hecke parameter, viewed as an element of $\mathbb C^\times$, and let $\xi\ne1$ be a root of unity in $\mathbb C$. With quantum characteristic as in [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], $e(\mathbb C,q)=\infty$ and $e(\mathbb C,\xi)$ is the finite multiplicative order of $\xi$. In particular $q\ne\xi$. The statement compares scalar parameter regimes; it asserts no isomorphism, Morita equivalence, or classification relation between the corresponding algebras.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Thus the p-adic positive-real parameter has infinite quantum characteristic and the finite type-A root-of-unity parameter has finite quantum characteristic $4$. Since $|3|=3$ and $|i|=1$, they are different scalars. These calculations establish only the stated parameter distinction.

A **root datum** is a quadruple $(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consisting of free $\mathbb Z$-modules $X,X^\vee$ of finite rank in perfect duality $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:X\times X^\vee\to\mathbb Z$, finite subsets $\Phi\subseteq X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subseteq X^\vee$, and a bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$ from $\Phi$ to $\Phi^\vee$, subject to (rd1) $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi$; (rd2) the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(y)=y-\langle\alpha,y\rangle\alpha^\vee$ satisfy $s_\alpha(\Phi)\subseteq\Phi$ and $s_{\alpha^\vee}(\Phi^\vee)\subseteq\Phi^\vee$; (rd3) the group $W(R)$ generated by the $s_\alpha$ acting on $X$ is finite. The root datum is **reduced** if $\mathbb Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\pm\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. The group $W(R)$ is the **Weyl group**, $\Phi$ the root system and $\Phi^\vee$ the coroot system; $W(R)$ acts dually on $X^\vee$ by the $s_{\alpha^\vee}$, and $s_\alpha$ fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$. For $V_{\mathbb R}=X\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R$, the **Weyl chambers** are the connected components of $V_{\mathbb R}\smallsetminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\{x:\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0\}$, and a **base** is a linearly independent subset $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ such that every root is a $\mathbb Z$-combination of $\Delta$ with all coefficients of one sign. A root datum is **semisimple** if $Z\Phi$ has finite index in $X$.

The reflection $s_\alpha$ depends only on the pair $(\alpha,\alpha^\vee)$: it fixes the hyperplane $\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, sends $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$ by (rd1), and is determined by those two conditions on the rational direct sum $\mathbb Q\alpha\oplus\ker(\langle\ ,\alpha^\vee\rangle:X\otimes\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q)$. The lattice form above is related to the Euclidean root-system theory of [[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]] and [[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]] through a $W$-invariant form on $V_{\mathbb R}$, but no choice of invariant inner product belongs to the definition. The perfect character–cocharacter pairing for a split torus is supplied by [[lem-character-and-cocharacter-lattices-of-a-split-torus]]; roots and coroots are additional data, not supplied by that lattice lemma.

An **isomorphism of root data** $R=(X,\Phi,X^\vee,\Phi^\vee)\to R_1=(X_1,\Phi_1,X_1^\vee,\Phi_1^\vee)$ is a pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear isomorphisms $f:X\to X_1$ and $f^\vee:X_1^\vee\to X^\vee$ that are transpose to one another, $\langle f(x),y_1\rangle=\langle x,f^\vee(y_1)\rangle$ for all $x\in X$, $y_1\in X_1^\vee$, and that carry $\Phi$ bijectively onto $\Phi_1$ with $f(\alpha)^\vee=f^\vee{} ^{-1}(\alpha^\vee)$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi$. Composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, with the evident inverses, so root data form a category whose isomorphisms are these pairs; this is the notion of isomorphism used when separating the root data of SL_2 and PGL_2.

Let $R=(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be a reduced based root datum: $X,Y$ are finite-rank free lattices in perfect integral duality, $\Phi\subset X$ is the finite root set, $\Phi^\vee\subset Y$ its coroot set, $\Delta$ a base, and $W_0$ the finite Weyl group ([[def-abstract-root-datum-and-its-weyl-group]]). Its finite simple-reflection set is $S_0:=\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}\subset W_0$; the simple reflections in a chosen base generate $W_0$ ([[lem-root-datum-combinatorics]]). Write $Q^\vee=\mathbb Z\Phi^\vee\subseteq Y$ for the coroot lattice.

Put $V=Y\otimes_\mathbb Z\mathbb R$. The **canonical affine walls** are $H_{\alpha,j}=\{v:\langle\alpha,v\rangle=j\}$, with reflection $r_{\alpha,j}(v)=v-(\langle\alpha,v\rangle-j)\alpha^\vee$. The base alcove $A$ is the unique alcove in the positive chamber with $0$ in its closure; equivalently $A$ is defined by $0<\langle\alpha,v\rangle<1$ for every positive root $\alpha$. If there are no roots, put $A=V$. For a nonsemisimple root datum the alcoves include the whole common root kernel as a factor. Define $W_{\mathrm{aff}}=Q^\vee\rtimes W_0$, let $S_{\mathrm{aff}}$ be its reflections in the walls of $A$, put $W_{\mathrm e}=Y\rtimes W_0$, and let $\Omega=\operatorname{Stab}_{W_{\mathrm e}}(A)$. The canonical affine Coxeter system and the decomposition $W_{\mathrm e}=W_{\mathrm{aff}}\rtimes\Omega$, including central lattice directions, are proved in [[lem-hh-root-datum-affine-geometry-and-wall-parameters]]. In particular $S_0\subset S_{\mathrm{aff}}$ with the finite Weyl product orders. Define length on $W_{\mathrm e}$ as the number of walls separating $A$ from its translate; on $W_{\mathrm{aff}}$ it is Coxeter length, and its zero set is $\Omega$. Thus no arbitrary nongeometric affine Coxeter extension is silently compared with the lattice below.

Choose a parameter function $q:S_{\mathrm{aff}}\to\mathbb R_{>0}$ invariant under conjugation by $W_{\mathrm e}$. For $s,t\in S_{\mathrm{aff}}$ with finite Coxeter label $m(s,t)$, impose the alternating braid relation with $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)$ to be the quotient of the free associative $\mathbb C$-algebra on $(T_s)_{s\in S_{\mathrm{aff}}}$ by those braid relations and

$$
(T_s-q_s)(T_s+1)=0\qquad(s\in S_{\mathrm{aff}}).
$$

The extended **Iwahori–Matsumoto affine Hecke algebra** is the crossed product $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q):=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)\rtimes\Omega$. Its underlying vector space is $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)\otimes_\mathbb C\mathbb C[\Omega]$, with multiplication $(hU_\omega)(h'U_\eta)=h\,\omega(h')U_{\omega\eta}$. Thus it adjoins symbols $U_\omega$ with $U_\omega U_\eta=U_{\omega\eta}$ and $U_\omega T_sU_\omega^{-1}=T_{\omega s\omega^{-1}}$. Parameter invariance makes each conjugation an algebra automorphism. If $v_s=\sqrt{q_s}>0$ and $N_s=q_s^{-1/2}T_s$, then $(N_s-v_s)(N_s+v_s^{-1})=0$, the symmetric normalization in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]].

This definition asserts neither an Iwahori–Matsumoto basis nor an equivalence with a Bernstein presentation. It does not identify an arbitrary reductive $p$-adic group's Iwahori-fixed category with modules over this algebra; that requires a separate group-specific equivalence.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with inner product $B$ ([[def-inner-product-space]]). Equip it with the induced norm $\|x\|_B=\sqrt{B(x,x)}$ ([[def-inner-product-norm]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) and metric $d_B(x,y)=\|x-y\|_B$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]); $\mathrm{Isom}(E)$ below means the isometry group for $d_B$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a supplied reduced crystallographic root system spanning $E$ ([[def-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]). For each $\alpha\in\Phi$, put $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/B(\alpha,\alpha)$ ([[def-coroot-and-dual-root-system]]); write $s_\alpha$ for the orthogonal reflection in the hyperplane $B(x,\alpha)=0$ and $W=W(\Phi)=\langle s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\rangle$ for the Weyl group ([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]]). Write $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$ for the root and coroot lattices ([[def-root-lattice-coroot-lattice-weight-lattice-and-coweight-lattice]]), and fix a positive system with base $\Delta=\{\alpha_s:s\in S\}$ ([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]).

For $\alpha\in\Phi$ and $k\in\mathbb Z$, define
$$H_{\alpha,k}:=\{x\in E:B(x,\alpha)=k\},\qquad r_{\alpha,k}(x):=x-\bigl(B(x,\alpha)-k\bigr)\alpha^\vee.$$
Each $H_{\alpha,k}$ is an affine hyperplane: $B(-,\alpha)$ is a nonzero linear functional, and $k\alpha/B(\alpha,\alpha)$ lies in its level-$k$ set. The sets $H_{\alpha,k}$ are the **affine root hyperplanes** or **walls**, and
$$\mathcal A_\Phi:=\{H_{\alpha,k}:\alpha\in\Phi,\ k\in\mathbb Z\}$$
is their **affine wall arrangement**. An **alcove** is a connected component of $E\setminus\bigcup\mathcal A_\Phi$, with the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]).

The **affine reflection group** $W_a$ is the subgroup of the Euclidean isometry group $\mathrm{Isom}(E)$ generated by the maps $r_{\alpha,k}$ ([[def-generated-subgroup]], [[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). The well-definedness obligation for this subgroup is assigned to `lem-cg-affine-reflection-identities-and-local-finiteness`, which verifies that each generator is an isometry. The **coroot translation group** is the image of the homomorphism $Q^\vee\to\mathrm{Isom}(E)$, $\lambda\mapsto t_\lambda$, where $t_\lambda(x)=x+\lambda$.

The Weyl group acts on $Q^\vee$ by $w\cdot\lambda:=w(\lambda)$. This action is by automorphisms: $W$ permutes $\Phi$, and for every root $\alpha$,
$$w(\alpha^\vee)=\frac{2w\alpha}{B(\alpha,\alpha)}=\frac{2w\alpha}{B(w\alpha,w\alpha)}=(w\alpha)^\vee,$$
so $w(Q^\vee)=Q^\vee$ and the restriction has inverse $w^{-1}|_{Q^\vee}$. These restrictions compose according to multiplication in $W$, giving the action required for the external semidirect product $Q^\vee\rtimes W$ ([[def-group-action]], [[def-action-by-automorphisms]], [[def-external-semidirect-product]]), whose multiplication is
$$(\lambda,w)(\mu,v)=(\lambda+w\mu,wv).$$

This item fixes the definitions and conventions. It does not assert $W_a=Q^\vee\rtimes W$, local finiteness of the arrangement, that alcoves are simplices, or that any specified alcove is a fundamental domain. The root system is supplied; no crystallographic scaling for a Coxeter matrix is constructed, and non-crystallographic types are outside this definition. No choice principle is used.

Use the affine-wall notation and componentwise fundamental alcove $A$ from [[def-cg-affine-root-hyperplane-reflection-and-alcove]] and [[lem-cg-highest-root-and-fundamental-alcove]]. Let $J$ be the affine facet-type set from [[lem-cg-affine-alcove-separation-and-facet-types]], with one label $0_i$ for each nonempty irreducible component, and let $s_a$ be the reflection in the fundamental facet of type $a\in J$. Let $W_{\rm abs}$, its Coxeter matrix $m_{ab}=\operatorname{ord}(s_as_b)$, and $\varphi:W_{\rm abs}\to W_a$ be those of [[lem-cg-affine-generic-gallery-paths-and-disk-moves]]; its finite labels are $2,3,4,6$, and $m_{ab}=\infty$ only for the two opposite facets of a rank-one component. If $J=\varnothing$, take $W_{\rm abs}=W_a=\{1\}$.

**(1) Transitivity and generation.** The subgroup $G:=\langle s_a:a\in J\rangle\le W_a$ equals $W_a$, and $W_a$ acts transitively on the set of alcoves. Every affine wall supports a facet of the closure of some alcove; if $H$ is a facet wall of $g(A)$, its reflection is $g s_a g^{-1}$ for the type $a$ of that facet.

**(2) Presentation and simple transitivity.** The homomorphism $\varphi:W_{\rm abs}\to W_a$ is an isomorphism. Thus $W_a$ is the Coxeter group with simple system $(s_a)_{a\in J}$, and it acts simply transitively on alcoves: for any two alcoves $C,C'$ there is exactly one $g\in W_a$ such that $g(C)=C'$.

**(3) Length.** Let $\ell(g)$ be the minimum number of facet reflections from $(s_a)_{a\in J}$ whose product is $g$. For every $g\in W_a$,
$$\ell(g)=\#\operatorname{Sep}(A,g(A)),$$
where $\operatorname{Sep}$ is the separating-wall set of [[lem-cg-affine-alcove-separation-and-facet-types]]. A straight generic segment between interior points of $A$ and $g(A)$ crosses each separating wall exactly once and gives a gallery attaining the minimum. The argument includes rank-one factors and reducible systems with the product conventions of [[lem-cg-highest-root-and-fundamental-alcove]] (3).

**(4) Comparison.** The finite root-system types are the standard crystallographic types $A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$ (with the low-rank identifications in [[thm-classification-of-irreducible-reduced-crystallographic-root-systems]]). In that root-system normalization, $W_a=Q^\vee\rtimes W$ from [[lem-cg-affine-reflection-identities-and-local-finiteness]] is the standard affine Weyl group. This does not identify it with an untwisted Kac–Moody loop realization, and it does not assert that the extended group $P^\vee\rtimes W$ is a Coxeter group with the same simple system. No axiom of choice is used.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group and $\ell$ its length function ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]). Write $s\sim t$ when there exist $s=s_0,s_1,\dots,s_k=t$ in $S$ with $m(s_i,s_{i+1})$ odd for every $i<k$; this is the connected-component relation of the graph on $S$ whose edges are the pairs with odd $m$, and it is an equivalence relation (1.1). Let $[s]$ denote the class of $s$ and let $c$ be the number of classes.

**Coefficient ring.** Put $R:=\mathbb Z[v_1^{\pm1},\dots,v_c^{\pm1}]=\Lambda_{\mathbb Z,c}$, the Laurent polynomial ring in $c$ variables ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2): a commutative ring in which every $v_i$ is a unit. Identify the classes with $\{1,\dots,c\}$ and put $v_s:=v_{[s]}\in R^\times$ for $s\in S$.

**The generic Hecke algebra.** Let $F:=R\langle T_s:s\in S\rangle$ be the free associative $R$-algebra on $S$ and let $I\subseteq F$ be the two-sided ideal generated ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]], part 2) by the **quadratic relations**
$$(T_s-v_s)(T_s+v_s^{-1})\qquad(s\in S)$$
and the **braid relations**
$$T_sT_tT_s\cdots=T_tT_sT_t\cdots\qquad(s\ne t,\ m(s,t)<\infty),$$
both alternating products having $m(s,t)$ factors. Define $H:=H(W):=F/I$ and write $T_s$ for the image of the generator $T_s$. Then $H$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) with the following **universal property**: for every unital associative $R$-algebra $A$ and every family $(t_s)_{s\in S}$ in $A$ satisfying the same two families of relations, there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $H\to A$ with $T_s\mapsto t_s$.

**Universal parameters.** For every commutative ring $A$ and units $u_1,\dots,u_c\in A^\times$ the assignment $v_i\mapsto u_i$ extends uniquely to a ring homomorphism $R\to A$ ([[lem-hh-finite-polynomial-and-localization-constructions]], part 2); via the universal property of $H$ this makes $R$ the universal coefficient ring for a unit-valued parameter that is constant on each class $[s]$.

**Generator conjugacy.** Two simple generators $s,t\in S$ are conjugate in $W$ if and only if $s\sim t$.

**Conventions and scope.** (i) $m(s,t)=\infty$ imposes no relation between $T_s$ and $T_t$; if $c=1$ we write $v$ for $v_1$. (ii) The quadratic relation is equivalent to $T_s^2-(v_s-v_s^{-1})T_s-1=0$, equivalently $(T_s+v_s^{-1})(T_s-v_s)=0$, and it depends on $v_s$ only through the difference $v_s-v_s^{-1}$ (1.6). (iii) No freeness, torsion-freeness, specialisation or basis property of $H$ is asserted here: the elements $T_w$ are introduced in [[lem-hh-reduced-word-independence-and-length-multiplication]], their independence is proved in [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], and the invertibility and bar properties are recorded in [[lem-hh-hecke-anti-involution-bar-and-normalization]]; consumers may not use those features before those items.

Let $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{aff}}(R,q)\rtimes\Omega$ be the Iwahori–Matsumoto algebra of [[def-hh-affine-hecke-algebra-from-root-datum]]. For $w\in W_{\mathrm{aff}}$, let $T_w$ be the product along a reduced expression, and let $U_\omega$ denote the length-zero symmetry corresponding to $\omega\in\Omega$. Then

$$
\{T_wU_\omega:w\in W_{\mathrm{aff}},\ \omega\in\Omega\}
$$

is a $\mathbb C$-basis of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{IM}}(R,q)$.

derivations.claim: The vectors $e_1$ and $\tfrac12(e_1+e_2)$ form a basis of $X$, while $e_1-e_2$ and $2e_2$ form a basis of $Y$: an integer pair $(a,b)$ has even coordinate sum exactly when $(a,b)=a(e_1-e_2)+\frac{a+b}{2}(2e_2)$. The dot-product matrix between these two bases is the identity, so the pairing is perfect and integral. The roots lie in $X$, the coroots lie in $Y$, and direct pairings on $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ give the Cartan matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The signed-permutation group generated by $s_1,s_2$ preserves both displayed root sets and is finite. Thus [F1] applies and these data are a reduced based $B_2$ root datum.

The simple walls of $\mathcal A_0$ are $x_1=x_2$, $x_2=0$, and $x_1+x_2=1$; the other positive-root functions $x_1$ and $x_1-x_2$ lie strictly between $0$ and $1$ in this region, so no other integer root wall cuts it. Their reflections are respectively the displayed $s_1,s_2,s_0$. The product $s_1s_2$ is $(x_1,x_2)\mapsto(-x_2,x_1)$, a quarter-turn of order $4$. The product $s_2s_0$ is $(x_1,x_2)\mapsto(1-x_2,x_1-1)$; it fixes $(1,0)$ and its linear part about that point is the same quarter-turn, so it has order $4$. The product $s_0s_1$ is $(x_1,x_2)\mapsto(1-x_1,1-x_2)$, a half-turn of order $2$. Hence the affine Coxeter labels are $m(s_1,s_2)=m(s_2,s_0)=4$ and $m(s_1,s_0)=2$.

The affine roots defining $s_0$ and $s_1$ are long and the one defining $s_2$ is short. The Coxeter labels just computed are all even, so the odd-edge graph has three singleton components. Therefore $q_{s_0}=2$, $q_{s_1}=2$, and $q_{s_2}=3$ are constant on every required component by [F4]. In the symmetric convention the corresponding parameters are $v_{s_0}=v_{s_1}=\sqrt2$ and $v_{s_2}=\sqrt3$, with the quadratic relations of [F2].

Here $Y=Q^\vee$, so the extended group has trivial length-zero quotient and $\Omega=\{1\}$. Applying [L1] to the affine Coxeter system identified in step 1.2, with the valid affine Coxeter parameters from step 2.1, shows that $\{T_w:w\in W_{\mathrm{aff}}\}$ is a $\mathbb C$-basis. This verifies the claimed unequal-parameter affine $B_2$ example.
